title: Indian Household Budgeting Framework & 50/30/20 Rule Adaptation
publisher: National Institute of Financial Management & Indian Personal Finance Standards
summary: Practical adaptation of proportional salary allocation (50/30/20) for Indian urban and semi-urban salary earners accounting for high essential overheads, medical buffers, and systematic savings.

chunks.title: Adapted 50/30/20 Proportional Allocation for Indian Households
chunks.text: The classic 50/30/20 rule is adapted for Indian cost structures as follows: 50% Net Inflow allocated to Essential Living Commitments (House Rent/Maintenance, Utility bills, Groceries, Children's school fees, Commute, Term/Health Insurance premiums, and existing Loan EMIs). 30% Net Inflow allocated to Discretionary Lifestyle Spending (Dining out, Entertainment, OTT subscriptions, Travel, Gadgets, and Shopping). 20% Net Inflow strictly allocated to Systematic Wealth Building & Goal Savings (SIP mutual funds, PPF, EPF contributions, NPS, and recurring deposits).

chunks.title: Safe-to-Spend Daily Formula and Liquidity Management
chunks.text: The Safe-to-Spend indicator represents true discretionary liquidity left in the current pay cycle after ring-fencing upcoming fixed obligations, pending essential bills, and mandatory savings targets. Safe-to-Spend per day is calculated by dividing total uncommitted surplus by remaining days until next salary credit. If safe-to-spend approaches zero, all non-essential dining and entertainment purchases must immediately pause to prevent debt reliance.

chunks.title: Tax-Efficient Savings Vehicles and Long-Term Buffers
chunks.text: Indian salary earners benefit from disciplined allocation into tax-advantaged instruments like Public Provident Fund (PPF - 15-year sovereign risk-free sovereign lock-in), Voluntary Provident Fund (VPF), and National Pension System (NPS). For emergency funds, capital should be held in High-Yield Savings Accounts or Instant Redemption Liquid Funds without tax friction upon emergency withdrawal.
